summary: Addresses how to discover URN resolver services, which translate Uniform Resource Names into URLs and other descriptions of a resource. It is informational and discusses architectural principles.

eli5.summary: A permanent name for something like a book is not an address. This talks about how to find the service that turns the name into where to get it.

questions: what is a resolver discovery service
what is a hint in urn resolution
subtitle: Design principles for finding the service that turns a permanent URN into a place where the resource can be fetched.

tldr.problem: URNs are meant to be persistent, globally unique names, but a client still has to find a resolver that can turn a URN into a URL or other description of where the resource lives.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out assumptions (persistence, delegation, independence), guidelines for a Resolver Discovery Service in three areas (evolvability, usability, security and privacy), and a loose framework in which a global registry of namespace identifiers points to rules or resolvers.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational set of engineering criteria, not a protocol. Meeting the framework does not by itself mean meeting the guidelines, and it was later updated by RFC 3401.

facts.label: Security guidelines named
facts.value: 3: access control, server authenticity, server distribution

today: RFC 2276 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 3401. The RFC itself offers criteria and a framework rather than a specified protocol.

sections.title: Resolver Discovery and Hints
sections.content:
The RFC lays out engineering criteria for a Resolver Discovery Service (RDS): a service that helps a client learn about URN resolvers. A resolver translates URNs into URLs or URCs (Uniform Resource Characteristics), and some also give direct access to the resource. The solution has to be globally scalable.

The URI working group concluded that a persistent, globally unique identifier, kept apart from location, was needed. These are URNs. They are meant for machines, and human-friendly names are a separate matter that this document leaves aside.

The central idea is the hint: anything that helps resolve a URN, such as the address of a resolver or a place the resource was previously found. Hints may be out of date or valid only locally, and they can carry meta-information such as an expiration time. Most resolutions are expected to use locally stored hints, and an RDS is the fall-back when those fail. The RFC also notes that a URN does not guarantee resolution everywhere or in the same way everywhere.
sections.eli5: A hint is like a note saying "try the library on Main Street." It usually helps, but it might be out of date. A discovery service is the person you ask when your notes do not work.

sections.title: The Three Assumptions
sections.content:
The design rests on three assumptions: longevity, delegation and independence.

Longevity. A URN is a persistent identifier that should outlast the resources, users and systems around it. Resources move, organizations merge and protocols change, so users and applications must stay independent of those changing details.

Delegation. Naming and resolution authorities may delegate parts of their authority, which the RFC calls the only known way to get the expected scale. It also stresses separating name assignment (labelling a resource with a URN) from name resolution (finding the resource given the URN), each with multi-tiered delegation.

Independence. A delegatee works independently of its peers and, within bounds, of the delegator. Publishers can choose resolver services, clients can choose among RDS services, security levels can be chosen independently, and a namespace owner can choose its own canonicalization rule. The modularity also gives some protection against denial of service.
sections.eli5: The name should last a long time, different people can be put in charge of different parts, and each person can make their own choices without asking everyone else.

sections.title: Guideline One: Evolvability
sections.content:
An RDS must be prepared for change. The guidelines call for scaling in three dimensions: the number of resources needing URNs, the number of publishers and users, and the complexity of delegation. The environment must also support a growing set of URN schemes, new kinds of local resolver services, new authentication schemes, and several RDS schemes running at the same time.

The RFC gives examples. A specialized resolver could exploit the structure of ISBNs for efficiency, while a general-purpose one could understand every URN scheme at average speed. No single authentication scheme is globally accepted, and old ones become too easy to spoof or guess.

Finally, an RDS must allow administrative control mechanisms to manage human behavior around limited resources. Pricing and administrative controls are named as two suggestions.
sections.eli5: Whatever system we build today, it has to be easy to swap parts and grow, because tomorrow's world will look different.

sections.title: Guideline Two: Usability for Each Participant
sections.content:
Usability is judged from three viewpoints: the publisher, the client and the management of the hint infrastructure.

Publishers need URN-to-hint resolution that is correct and efficient with very high probability. They must be able to move between resolver services, arrange multiple access points, provide hints with both long and short lifetimes, and easily state and check their hint information and security constraints. Different clients may be given different hints, which has implications for caching.

Clients need a simple, efficient interface and hints they can understand, so they can set preferences and priorities. The RFC expects people to deal mostly with human-friendly names, and says mapping those to URNs stays a separate function from an RDS.

Management of hints must be unobtrusive and use few network resources. Administrative incentives such as a small one-time charge for storing a hint can encourage one general hint over many specific ones. Servers must also be simple to configure and verify.
sections.eli5: The people who post things, the people who look for them, and the people running the help desk all need it to be easy and not a burden on anyone.

sections.title: Guideline Three: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The security guidelines are all phrased as "it must be possible" because needs differ between clients. They cover creating authoritative hints with controlled modification, determining a server's identity or avoiding unauthenticated ones, reducing denial of service by broad distribution, some privacy for traffic, letting publishers keep information such as their client list private, and letting publishers restrict access to resolution of their URNs.

The RFC defines "authoritative" in the security sense: it means a principal with the right to approve the hint has done so, not that the hint is correct. It names three security guidelines in particular: access control on hints, server authenticity, and server distribution. A client that receives unvalidated information should treat the hint as possibly inaccurate.

Because hints are by nature not guaranteed correct, the RFC says it is unlikely to be worth heavy expense on their correctness. Publishers who want a private name should not expect a public RDS to serve them. Access control over resolution is better provided by the publisher's own resolver servers than by an RDS.
sections.eli5: People should be able to check who is giving them directions and who is allowed to change the directions. Anything truly secret should be kept behind the owner's own door, not at the public help desk.

sections.title: The Framework
sections.content:
The framework bounds the search space for RDS designs. It builds on the URN syntax URN:<NID>:<NSS> from RFC 2141, where NID is the namespace identifier and NSS is the namespace specific string. The NID sets the top-level syntax and tells the client how to pick the first server to contact.

Resolution starts at a Global NID registry, which returns either a rule or a reference to a URN resolver service. At each stage, a rule yields the identity of another RDS server (and possibly a string to look up), or a reference outside the RDS leads to a resolver service and ends use of the RDS.

The framework leaves open the protocols, data organization, replication, where rule computations run, how the registry is reached, and whether the database is partitioned along naming-authority boundaries. More than one RDS may coexist so the system can evolve, and information should be available through any operational one. The RFC is explicit that following the framework does not guarantee meeting the guidelines, so compliance must be evaluated separately and any shortfall documented.
sections.eli5: Start at one big phone book of name types. It tells you either the answer or which smaller phone book to open next, until you reach someone who can actually help.

items.title: Access control on hints
items.text: An authoritative hint can be changed only by principals with the right to modify it, as chosen by the publisher.

items.title: Server authenticity
items.text: Servers and clients must be able to learn the identity of the servers they talk to.

items.title: Server distribution
items.text: Broad availability resists denial of service and reduces trust in any single server.
